subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: contingency planning for weather and delays [Thinking]
passage: In their Mumbai flat, Deepika and Ritu went over the plan for the sangeet: an evening function on the lawn, in July. "What if it rains?" Ritu asked. "It's Mumbai. It will." Deepika wrote two words at the bottom of the list: Plan B. They booked the banquet room next door for the same evening for a small fee, sketched how the stage and chairs would move inside, and kept a little money aside for anything unexpected. On the day, clouds rolled in at five. The banquet staff had been told, and the decor team knew the order of moves. In an hour the stage stood indoors and the guests were finding their seats. Ritu's mother whispered, "Was this planned?" Deepika grinned. "Just in case."

qa.q: Where was the indoor Plan B booked?
qa.a: The indoor Plan B was the banquet room next door.

qa.q: How did Deepika probably feel when the clouds rolled in?
qa.a: Deepika was probably calm and quietly pleased, since the plan was ready.

qa.q: What else could Deepika and Ritu prepare for, and why?
qa.a: They could also plan for a late vendor or a power cut, because contingency thinking covers other likely surprises as well as rain.

qa.q: How might Ritu's mother have felt as the stage moved indoors?
qa.a: Ritu's mother was probably surprised and relieved that nothing had turned into a crisis, and curious about how the move had been arranged.

grounding: Illustrates preparing an indoor option for an outdoor function in monsoon and keeping a small reserve, so a rain shift takes an hour instead of a crisis.

subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: pausing to reset after a conflict over guests [Revision]
passage: Pradeep, you look tense about your guest list, so let me tell you what my husband and I did. I'm Shreya. Ten days before our wedding we had a shouting match over it. He wanted a hundred and fifty, and I had found myself adding relatives until it reached three hundred. I walked out to the balcony, he stayed in the kitchen, and we didn't speak for an hour. Then he came out with two cups of tea. We set a cap of two hundred and a rule: exceptions only if both of us agreed. The next day we sat with each set of parents and said why: "We want to be able to talk with everyone who comes." Both families listened. It hurt less because we had both stopped fighting first.

qa.q: What cap did the couple set for the guests?
qa.a: They set a cap of two hundred.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel on walking out to the balcony?
qa.a: Shreya was upset and frustrated after the shouting match, and needed a pause before speaking again.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped end the fight, and why?
qa.a: Stopping for an hour and then agreeing a cap with a rule for exceptions helped, because it replaced arguing about numbers with a shared limit.

qa.q: How might Shreya's husband have felt when he brought out the two cups of tea?
qa.a: He probably felt regret and a wish to make peace, offering tea as a way to reopen the conversation.

grounding: Illustrates a couple stepping back after a heated fight over the guest list, agreeing a cap and a rule for exceptions and explaining it kindly to both families.

subtype: Approach: laying out all income, debts and goals openly [Thinking]
passage: In the waiting area of the bank branch, token number 42 was still glowing red, so Nikita took out a notebook. "Before we open the joint account, let's put everything on paper," she said. Nilesh turned to a blank page. Salaries first. Then Nikita's education loan payment and Nilesh's two-wheeler loan. Then the savings in a recurring deposit, and the plan to rent a bigger flat next year. As the page filled, Nilesh laughed softly. "I thought you had far more debt than this." "I thought the same about you," Nikita said. Their token was called. They walked to the counter like two people on the same team, who could finally reason with facts and not with guesses.

qa.q: What plan did Nikita and Nilesh write down for next year?
qa.a: They wrote down the plan to rent a bigger flat next year.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when the page filled with numbers?
qa.a: Nilesh was relieved and amused, since the debts were smaller than imagined.

qa.q: What else could Nikita and Nilesh do with the list, and why?
qa.a: They could set a time to update it together after a few months, because incomes, loans and plans change.

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt when Nilesh said that?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt relieved as well, since the same worry had been on both sides.

grounding: Illustrates a newly married couple openly listing salaries, loan payments, savings and plans so they can reason as one team rather than guess about each other.

subtype: Approach: three-account structure of joint and personal money [Action]
passage: Rehana, you asked how my husband and I avoid fights about money. I'm Gurleen. When we married, we set up three accounts. One joint account for rent, bills and groceries. Each of us put in a share that matched our income, not half and half: he earned more then, so he put in more. And two personal accounts, for anything we liked, with no explaining. My first buy from mine was a set of oil paints I'd never have justified to anyone. That is what I mean: safe together, free apart. It wasn't perfect, and we adjusted the shares when my income grew. But it saved us from a great many arguments, and neither of us ever felt watched.

qa.q: What goes into the joint account?
qa.a: The joint account is for rent, bills and groceries.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel about the personal account?
qa.a: Gurleen felt free and pleased, buying oil paints with no need to justify it.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept the arrangement fair, and why?
qa.a: Putting in a share matching each income, not half and half, kept it fair, because each person's contribution fitted what they earned.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's husband have seen the shares matching income?
qa.a: He probably saw it as fair and steady, since he put in more when he earned more and the shares changed when Gurleen's income grew.

grounding: Illustrates a couple with a joint account for rent and bills funded in proportion to income, plus separate personal accounts, giving shared security and individual freedom.

subtype: Approach: setting a monthly money meeting [Action]
passage:
Subject: Our Sunday meeting

Usha,

Thank you for sitting down with me on Sunday. Thirty minutes, tea, one notebook. I didn't expect to enjoy it. Let's keep it going: the first Sunday of every month. We go through what we spent, what is coming up, and anything either of us is unsure about. The point isn't to check on each other. It's so that a small worry gets said out loud in April instead of turning into a fight in July, and so that neither of us gets caught off guard by a large buy. Next time I'll make the tea, and you bring the notebook.

Nilesh

qa.q: On which day of the month will they hold the meeting?
qa.a: They will hold it on the first Sunday of every month.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel about the first meeting?
qa.a: Nilesh feels pleasantly surprised, having expected not to enjoy it.

qa.q: What could Nilesh and Usha do if they disagree about a purchase in the meeting, and why?
qa.a: They could pause the decision until the next Sunday, because time to think keeps a small disagreement from turning into a fight.

qa.q: How might Usha feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Usha probably feels reassured and appreciated, since the email says the aim is to share worries early and not to check on each other.

grounding: Illustrates setting a monthly money meeting on the first Sunday so small problems are discussed early and neither partner is ambushed by a big purchase.

subtype: Approach: values-first planning about saving versus spending [Thinking]
passage:
Amandeep: I keep saying flat, flat, flat. You keep saying trip. That's the fourth time we've had this fight.
Bhupen: Because a life without trips isn't one I want to save for.
Amandeep: And to me the flat is the reason we work.
Bhupen: What if we stop arguing about who's right and ask what each thing is for? For me a trip is feeling free.
Amandeep: And the flat is feeling safe.
Bhupen: Then what if sixty percent of what we set aside goes to the flat, and forty to travel?
Amandeep: Sixty and forty. Can we look at it again in a year?
Bhupen: Deal. One good trip a year is still real.
Amandeep: And I don't feel I've lost the flat.

qa.q: What split did Amandeep and Bhupen agree on?
qa.a: They agreed on sixty percent to the flat and forty to travel.

qa.q: What does the flat mean to Amandeep, and how does Amandeep feel about it?
qa.a: The flat means feeling safe to Amandeep, and Amandeep is relieved that it has not been given up.

qa.q: What else could the couple do to keep the agreement working, and why?
qa.a: They could review it after a year as agreed and note what each goal has given them, because priorities may shift.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when the trip was kept in the plan?
qa.a: Bhupen was probably relieved and appreciated, since travel stayed a real part of the plan and not a dismissed wish.

grounding: Illustrates a couple with different money priorities agreeing a percentage for each goal after asking what saving and travel mean to each, so neither feels dismissed.

subtype: Approach: one partner managing everything without discussion [Pitfall]
passage:
I thought I was being kind. When we married, I took all the money matters: the loans, the savings, the bills, the tax forms. It was easier that way, I told myself, and Rajni never asked. Then in March a big repair bill for our flat's roof arrived after the rains. Rajni asked where we stood, and I said, "Don't worry about it." She said, "I don't know what we owe or what we have." She wasn't angry so much as hurt. Looking back, keeping everything to myself wasn't ease. It was a kind of control I'd never named. It took us months of small, awkward talks to rebuild trust.

Hemant

qa.q: Which money matters did Hemant take on?
qa.a: Hemant took on the loans, the savings, the bills and the tax forms.

qa.q: How does Hemant feel now, looking back on keeping the money matters alone?
qa.a: Hemant now feels regret and recognises it as a kind of control, not the kindness it seemed to be.

qa.q: What could Hemant have done differently at the start, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could have shown Rajni the accounts and the loans and shared the tasks, because knowing the full picture lets both handle a sudden expense together.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when told not to worry about the repair bill?
qa.a: Rajni probably felt hurt and left out, not knowing what the couple owed or had.

grounding: Illustrates one partner managing all money without discussion, so the other does not know the loans or savings, and a sudden expense causes tension and mistrust.

subtype: Approach: hiding a debt or spending to avoid a fight [Pitfall]
passage: The statement came in a brown envelope on a Tuesday, and Karthik slid it under the mattress. The balance was larger than Wasim knew: restaurant dinners, a phone upgrade, a friend's trip. Karthik planned to clear it in three months from the bonus, quietly, before it ever came up. The bonus was delayed. In the fourth month the bank phoned the landline while Karthik was out, and Wasim answered. That evening the brown envelope lay open on the table. "It isn't the amount," Wasim said. "I can deal with an amount. It's that you hid it." Karthik had no reply. Over the next months the balance went down far faster than the trust came back.

qa.q: Where did Karthik hide the statement?
qa.a: Karthik slid the statement under the mattress.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling while hiding the balance?
qa.a: Karthik felt worried and ashamed, hoping to clear the balance quietly from the bonus before it ever came up.

qa.q: What could Karthik have done when the statement arrived, and why?
qa.a: Karthik could have shown Wasim the statement and made a repayment plan together, because the amount is easier to face than the loss of trust.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel on finding the envelope?
qa.a: Wasim was hurt more by the hiding than by the amount, and the hurt showed in the words that the amount can be dealt with.

grounding: Illustrates concealing a credit card balance in the hope of clearing it quietly, so that when it comes out the concern shifts from the amount to broken trust.

passage:
Sunday. Three colleagues have new cars and a fourth just came back from a beach holiday. Nazia said, "We're behind, aren't we?" and I said, "A bit." So this quarter we upgraded the phones, booked the beach trip and leased a car. I never opened the budget sheet. Tonight the card app showed the balance and my stomach dropped. It's the second card we've had to use in three months. We argued for an hour over whose idea it was, and both of us said, "You started it." I don't even like the car that much. I keep picturing our friends' photos, and I have no idea what their finances look like. Tomorrow I'll open the sheet.

Pradeep

qa.q: How many cards have Pradeep and Nazia had to use in three months?
qa.a: They have had to use the second card in three months.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel when the card app shows the balance?
qa.a: Pradeep feels anxious and regretful, with a dropping stomach, and admits not even liking the car much.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep and Nazia do before spending again, and why?
qa.a: They could check their own budget sheet together before any purchase, because a plan built on friends' lifestyles ignores their own income.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt during the hour-long argument?
qa.a: Nazia was probably tense and defensive, and stressed about the balance, since both of them said, "You started it."

grounding: Illustrates a couple raising their spending after seeing colleagues' cars and holidays without checking their own budget, ending up on credit cards and arguing.

subtype: Approach: building an emergency fund first [Action]
passage: In their two-room rented home in a mill town, Ujjwal and Sabina both wanted a small plot and a scooter. "First," Sabina said, "six months of what we spend, in an account we can reach any day." It took two years, setting aside a fixed sum on the day the salary arrived. Then the mill announced a shutdown for repairs, and Ujjwal was sent home without pay for two months. He sat on the doorstep, quiet. Sabina brought tea and the bank passbook. "We can manage." They paid rent and food from the fund and asked nobody for a loan. When the mill reopened, they started on the plot fund again, a little wiser and a lot calmer.

qa.q: How many months of spending did Sabina want in the account first?
qa.a: Sabina wanted six months of what they spend.

qa.q: How was Ujjwal feeling when he sat quietly on the doorstep?
qa.a: Ujjwal was worried and low after the mill sent him home without pay, until Sabina showed the passbook and said they could manage.

qa.q: What else could the couple do with the fund, and why?
qa.a: They could keep it apart from everyday money and check it once a year, because money that is easy to reach for other things may not be there in an emergency.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt handing over the passbook?
qa.a: Sabina was probably relieved and quietly proud that the years of setting money aside had paid off.

grounding: Illustrates a couple holding six months of expenses in an easily reached account before big goals, so a job scare later passes without borrowing.
